LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

Grapes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson snacks its way through the letter: your child makes the guh sound at the back of their mouth, counts grapes one guh at a time, and traces a letter with a tail.

What is this?

G is the seventh letter of the alphabet. In grapes, it makes its hard sound: guh — the back-of-the-mouth sound at the start of goose and giggle. The throat does the work; the lips stay out of it.

What does it mean?

G is a snack-table word, which means the practice renews itself several times a day without a lesson plan in sight. Letters attached to food get more rehearsal than any worksheet could buy.

What does the child need to know?

The letter is called G; in grapes it says guh — short and clean, made at the back. G owns a second sound, the j in giant, but grapes keeps today simple: one fruit, one sound.

Why this matters

Snacks arrive daily and grapes rarely miss a week, so this card earns more repetitions than almost any other in the set. Frequency, not cleverness, is what makes a letter sound stick.

What it teaches

Back-of-mouth sound production, one-to-one counting paired with sound, letter recognition in two cases, pincer-grip snack handling, and the patience of waiting for a counted treat.

Words to learn

Ggrapesguhcountsnackbunch

Say this to your child

“"This is the letter G — hello, G! G says guh, right at the back of your mouth, like a tiny gulp. Say it with me — guh, guh, grapes! Now count the plate with me: one guh, two guh, three guh... and eat the counting! Then trace the big G — round and round, with a little tail at the end."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and name the pair: this is the letter G, and this is a bunch of grapes — say grapes slowly and let guh stand up at the front.
  2. Make the sound at the back of your mouth: guh, like a gentle gulp. Try guh three times, then guh-grapes, feeling the throat do the work.
  3. Trace big G — a round curve that grows a small tail at the end — and little g: a circle with a tail that dangles below the line.
  4. Count grapes onto a little plate: one guh, two guh, three guh — one sound per grape, then eat the counting one grape at a time.
  5. End with a guh-hunt around the room: a toy goose, a giggle on demand, somebody’s grandpa in a photo — collect three and give each a clean guh.

Look closer at the picture

Find the big uppercase G and the little lowercase g on the card, then the bunch of grapes and the word Grapes. Ask which letter grew a tail — big G’s curve ends in a small hook, little g’s tail hangs below.

Ask your child

"What is this letter called?" "What does G say in grapes?" "Where do you feel the sound — front or back of your mouth?" "How many grapes shall we count next?" — answered with a name, a back-of-mouth guh, a hand on the throat and a number.

What your child can say or do

"Guh! Guh-grapes!" Expect grape-counting requests at snack time, guh-sounds offered to grandparents and garden hoses, and tails added to every circle your child draws. G is the letter that eats its homework.

Out in the real world

G grows through daily life: grapes, goose, giggle, gate, grandma. Every guh at the table or the garden gate is the card repeating itself — and snack counters never seem to tire of it.

Try it together

Grape counting shop: your child arranges six grape halves on a plate as the shopkeeper, you order one guh, two guh, three guh — and only sound-perfect counting gets the order filled. Swap roles; the shopkeeper may demand payment in guh-sounds.

Understanding check

Ask what G says in grapes: a clean back-of-mouth guh means the hard sound landed. A little g traced in the air — circle first, dangling tail second — completes the lesson.

Parent tips

G’s j-sound in giant or giraffe can stay a mystery for another year — if it comes up, "G has two costumes; today it wears the grape one" settles it cheerfully. Counted snacks end when the plate is empty, not before.

Staying safe

Whole grapes are a choking risk for under-fours — halve them lengthways before any counting game, and keep eating sitting-down. Washed hands, washed grapes, and the game pauses until every mouth is empty.

This lesson pairs with the Grapes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).
